Background

Joro spiders (Trichonephila clavata) are coming to New York!

Originally from Asia, this spider was first observed in Georgia, USA, circa 2010. Recent modeling studies have suggested the species could thrive in New York (Nelsen et al. 2023).

Given the pending (or already happened?) invasion, ecologists are studying the Joro spider more and more.

1

One explanation for the species rapid spread is the specific population that arrived in the United States differs from other populations of Joro spiders. For example, they may differ in their use of ballooning. Ballooning occurs when spiders deploy silk threads to catch air currents and disperse. In Joro spider populations in Japan, 18% of the hatchlings disperse via ballooning. An inital study of Joro spider hatchlings in Georgia indicated 22 out of 85 used ballooning. Does this suggest any difference in the use of ballooning by Joro spiders in Georgia?

Analyze the data. Make sure you include

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

    • *the proportion of spiders balloowing is equal to .18*

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

    • *the proportion of spiders balloowing is not equal to .18*

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

    • Since we have 2 outcomes and are comparing to a set proportion, I will use a binomial test.

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

 binom.test(22,85,.18)

    Exact binomial test

data:  22 and 85
number of successes = 22, number of trials = 85, p-value = 0.06593
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.18
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1698505 0.3652356
sample estimates:
probability of success 
             0.2588235

  • clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses (1.5 point)

    • Given a p-value of .06, I fail to reject the null hypothesis.

2

While presenting their work at a conference, another scientist shared they had done a similar but larger study. They found that 110 out of 425 hatchlings from Georgia used ballooning. What does their data indicate (you can use the same assumption of 18%)?

Analyze the data. Make sure you include

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

    • *the proportion of spiders balloowing is equal to .18*

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

    • *the proportion of spiders balloowing is not equal to .18*

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

    • Since we have 2 outcomes and are comparing to a set proportion, I will use a binomial test.

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

 binom.test(110, 425, .18)

    Exact binomial test

data:  110 and 425
number of successes = 110, number of trials = 425, p-value = 5.021e-05
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.18
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2178109 0.3032305
sample estimates:
probability of success 
             0.2588235

  • clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses (1.5 point)

    • Given a p-value of 0.0005, I reject the null hypothesis.

3

A new student is confused when comparing these studies. Both have the same signal for ballooning.

a

What is the signal for ballooning rate in both datasets?

110/425
[1] 0.2588235
22/85
[1] 0.2588235

Both samples shows a signal (proportion ballooning) of .258 #

b

However, they differ in p-value. Why? In answering this make sure you can explain what a p-value is.

The samples differ in associated p-values due to sample size. P-value is the probability of getting the signal you observed or something more extreme if the null hypothesis is true and you sampled the population multiple times.

4

The larger study also recorded hatchling sex (recorded as male or female). Data is shown below

Spider hatchling gender and ballooning
Sex
Use of ballooning Male Female
Ballooned 54 56
Did not balloon 150 175

How would you analyze the data to determine if sex impacts ballooning? Make sure you include

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

    • ballooning is not continget on sex

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

    • ballooning is continget on sex

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

  • clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses (1.5 point)

chisq.test(matrix(c(54, 56, 150,165), nrow = 2, byrow = T))

    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  matrix(c(54, 56, 150, 165), nrow = 2, byrow = T)
X-squared = 0.024079, df = 1, p-value = 0.8767

5

Another, related hypothesis is that the invasive spiders have smaller hatchlings. Weight data was collected from a population in Georgia and two populations in Asia (Japan and Korea). It can be loaded using. Weight is in mg.

set.seed(29)
spider_mass <- data.frame(population = c(rep("Georgia", 30), rep("Japan", 29), rep("Korea", 30)), mass_mg = c(rnorm(30, .25, .05), rnorm(30, .35, .07), rnorm(29, .32, .04)))
write.csv(spider_mass, "spider_mass.csv", row.names = F)
rm(spider_mass)
spider_mass <- read.csv("spider_mass.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)

How would you analyze the data. Make sure you include

  • null hypothesis (1 point)

  • alternative hypothesis (1 point)

  • explanation for test you will use (1.5 point)

  • results from statistical test (1 point)

  • clear explanation of how results relate to your stated hypotheses (1.5 point)

spider_mass_model <- lm(mass_mg~population, spider_mass)
plot(spider_mass_model)

6

Plot the data from question 5.

Several options here

library(Rmisc)
Loading required package: lattice
Loading required package: plyr
library(ggplot2)
Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3
spider_summary <- summarySE(spider_mass, measurevar="mass_mg", groupvars="population")
ggplot(spider_summary, aes(x=population, y=mass_mg)) +
    geom_point(size=3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=mass_mg - ci, ymax=mass_mg + ci), width=0) +
    ylab("Hatchling mass (mg)") +
    xlab("Population") +
    ggtitle("Hatchling Mass by Population") +
    theme(axis.title.x = element_text(face="bold", size=28),
          axis.title.y = element_text(face="bold", size=28),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size=20),
          axis.text.y = element_text(size=20),
          plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5, face="bold", size=32))
ggplot(spider_mass, aes(y=mass_mg, x=population, color=population)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  labs(title="Spider Masses in mg from Japan, Korea, and Georgia",
       y= "Spider weight (mg)",
       x= "population")+
  guides(color=F)
